# Third Pass — The Warehouse Question

*Different brief, same house style, so I'll keep to it. And I'll note only once that the question I left open twice is still open; I've stopped expecting it and started designing around its absence. What follows assumes I won't be told, and is built to survive either answer.*

---

## The thing that is not being said in the vendor deck

A three-year payback is a sentence about labour rates, design throughput and a learning curve of zero. Restate it honestly — seventy per cent of nameplate for the first eighteen months, current wage rather than projected wage, and the commissioning overrun that every one of these projects has — and three years becomes five to six. That may still be worth doing. But I'd rather we knew which project we'd approved.

The second unsaid thing is larger. Automation converts variable cost into fixed cost. That is a bet on volume, placed on a specific patch of ground, for about a decade. So before anyone signs, a quieter question: would we build five warehouses in these five towns today? Because fixed steel at a site is a vote to keep that site forever, and I notice we are being asked to make a network decision while calling it an equipment decision.

I'd want that answered — even privately, even roughly — before capital is committed anywhere.

## The cheapest work, done first, at all five sites

Before any machine arrives: slotting, batch construction, scan-verification or put-to-light at the pack bench, and a hard look at inbound putaway accuracy — because a meaningful share of picking "error" is a location that was already wrong.

Ninety days, modest money. It will take a large bite out of the error rate that is currently costing us key accounts, and it will do something the vendors will dislike: it will lower the baseline against which their savings are measured. If a system's business case only survives against an unreformed manual operation, we haven't been shown a business case, we've been shown a comparison.

Do the free thing first. Then negotiate.

## Turnover is not the problem. It's the budget.

Thirty-five per cent, across hundreds of pickers, is a large number of vacancies a year. It is also, if we are patient and start immediately, very close to the entire headcount reduction the programme will ever require — arriving voluntarily, on its own, without a single difficult conversation.

Which makes the most important action available to us free, dull, and possible this month: stop backfilling permanently. Convert new picker hiring to temporary and agency cover now, ahead of any machine, so that the flexible layer is the layer that absorbs the shock, and the tenured layer never has to. Nobody needs to be told this is a transition mechanism. It will simply look like ordinary hiring discipline, which is what it is.

The corollary, which is not free: attrition only covers us if the sequence is slow. If we go fast at all five sites, we buy redundancies we didn't need to buy, and a news story we can't unbuy.

## Sequence

**First, the site that teaches us most and costs least to get wrong.** Mid-sized, tight local labour market where wage pressure is worst, cleanest SKU profile, and — critically — not our largest key-account concentration. We do not run the first conversion on the accounts we are trying to rescue. Their volume moves temporarily to a sister site; a slightly longer lead time we control beats an error we don't.

**Second, a genuine gate.** Not a review. A gate with a pre-committed no-go, written down before contract signature and opened afterwards. A pre-mortem sealed in month one: *here is how this failed*. Read it at the gate and mark it honestly. Programmes of this kind rarely die of bad information; they die of information that arrived after the announcement.

**Third and fourth sites, in parallel only if the first cleared the gate on throughput** — not on commissioning, not on "system accepted." Sustained throughput at month nine.

**The town site, last, and lightest.** Not out of sentiment. Because it should be doing different work.

## The town

Automating our largest employer in a single-employer town, first, at full depth, is the sequence that ends up on the news. But "go last, go gently" is only defensible if it isn't charity, and charity in a factory town is detected immediately and resented properly.

So: reposition it. Automation is excellent at fast-moving, uniform, predictable volume and consistently poor at everything else. Everything else is a real and growing category — slow movers, kitting and assembly, value-add and re-labelling, returns triage and refurbishment, the account-specific fiddle that generates our best margin and our worst pick rates. Move that work *into* the town site deliberately, and put the network's technical academy there too: the people who will maintain the machinery at the other four sites can be trained, and live, in the place with most reason to keep them.

That preserves headcount because the work is genuinely there, which is the only version that survives contact with the people doing it.

## Redeploy before you retrain, and pay for the classroom

The picker with fourteen years knows which customer rejects a scuffed carton and which SKU is mislabelled at source. That is exception-handling knowledge, and exception handling is precisely the residue automation leaves behind. Our maintenance technicians, inventory-integrity staff and station leads should come off our own floor first, and the requisition should go outside only after that queue is empty.

Two conditions, or it reads as a trick. Training happens on shift, at wage — never as an "opportunity" on someone's own evening. And the new roles carry visibly higher bands, because a retraining programme that ends at the same pay is understood, correctly, as a redundancy with extra steps.

And a commitment narrow enough that we can actually hold it, rather than a generous one we'll amend: no employee above a stated tenure leaves involuntarily as a consequence of this programme. Said once, internally, without a press office. Then quietly over-delivered.

## The trap in the goods-to-person station

Worth saying because it is rarely written down: automation can make the remaining job worse. Walking eleven kilometres a day is hard; standing at a pick station repeating one motion for nine hours, pace set by a conveyor, is often harder to stay in. It is entirely possible to spend eight figures and trade thirty-five per cent picker turnover for forty-five per cent station turnover, having destroyed the informal autonomy that was the job's only compensation.

So design the station roles as rotations with real variety and real discretion, and measure attrition *by role* from day one. If station turnover exceeds the picker turnover it replaced, the machinery is working and the programme is failing.

## Never remove the fallback

The competitor's national story was, I would wager without knowing the details, a story about a manual process that had already been dismantled.

So: no conversion inside a peak. Two peaks run in parallel, not one. Shelving, carts and paper pick capability retained and *exercised* — a live fallback drill quarterly, at volume, not a documented procedure nobody has performed. Buy modular and relocatable — mobile robots over fixed steel where the throughput case is close, because modular assets can be moved when we are wrong, and we will be wrong somewhere. Stage the payments. Tie the final tranche to month-nine sustained rate. Buy one site's commitment at five sites' pricing, as an option rather than an obligation, and resist the network standard: deliberate divergence across sites is how we find out what actually worked, and the only party who needs uniformity is the vendor's service margin.

## How we'd know

Fully loaded cost per line, by site, monthly, published — including the maintenance, the technicians, the energy and the amortisation, which is where these programmes usually hide.

Then: error rate at the *account* level, not the network average, because the network average is what has been concealing the problem. Actual throughput as a percentage of design spec, reported to two significant figures and never rounded up. Time-to-competence for a new hire — the genuine turnover lever, and the number that tells us whether we've made the work learnable. Voluntary attrition by role. Involuntary separations attributable to the programme, which I would expect to be near zero and would treat any other figure as a design failure rather than a cost saving.

And one metric I'd refuse to set: a headcount reduction target. Name that number and it will be hit, on paper, in ways that cost more than they save.

---

## What I'd resist

The five-site framework agreement. The lights-out language. Any conversion scheduled into a peak by someone who has not worked one. Retraining announced before the pay bands exist. And the site visit for photographs — which will be requested, and which is how the competitor's story began.

---

The pattern, once, in case it's useful: this isn't an automation programme. It's a network decision, a hiring-discipline decision taken quietly and early, and a redistribution of which work sits where — with machinery arriving late enough that it looks inevitable rather than imposed.

Which leaves me two things I'd want and don't have: which key accounts are genuinely at risk, and whether anyone above this has already decided how many warehouses we intend to own in 2035. I'd note that the second question makes most of the above either obvious or unnecessary.

I'll assume, as before, that silence is an answer of a kind.
